title: Write Like Me: verified research register
scope: Stylometry; AI-text detection and its limitations; co-writing; style transfer; personalization; preference optimization; corpus vocabulary; multilingual evaluation; decoding and evaluation.

search_method.approach: Targeted title/author searches, followed by opening publisher/proceedings pages or primary article PDFs. Official publication records resolve preprint-versus-publication status.
search_families: authorship attribution survey function words stylometry
DetectGPT Fast-DetectGPT non-native English detector bias detector stress testing
CoAuthor LaMP TextSETTR style transfer evaluation
search_method.inclusion: Relevant original research or foundational synthesis with verified bibliographic metadata and an opened primary paper or official abstract/record.
search_method.exclusion: Vendor rankings, blogs, social posts, unverified citations, and papers whose only accessible evidence was a secondary summary.
limitations: No preregistration, exhaustive database export, duplicate screening, formal risk-of-bias instrument, or meta-analysis.
This selection is not a claim to cover all work through the review date; papers selected span 2009–2025.
Abstract-level records support only bounded summaries; no replication or quantitative pooling was performed.
All included entries have published peer-reviewed venues; historical arXiv versions are not separate evidence.
No private user writing was read; no personalized model or detector was tested.

papers.title: A survey of modern authorship attribution methods
papers.venue: Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 60(3), 538–556
papers.research_question: How are authorial text representations and classifiers evaluated?
papers.method: Surveys computational representations, classification settings, and evaluation practices.
papers.key_findings: Authorship analysis depends on task settings and evaluation methodology.
papers.limitations: Pre-LLM survey; no validation of this project or generative personalization.
papers.project_implication: Use interpretable features with documented samples and held-out evaluation.

notes: Issue year is 2009; publisher gives first online publication as 16 December 2008.
Only publisher abstract and bibliographic record were accessible; no exhaustive full-text claim.

papers.title: Function Words in Authorship Attribution. From Black Magic to Theory?
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Computational Linguistics for Literature (CLFL), 59–66
papers.research_question: Why do function-word features help stylometry?
papers.method: Theoretical discussion connecting frequent grammatical items and character n-grams.
papers.key_findings: Feature choices need explanation; striking rare words can reflect topic or genre.
papers.limitations: Position paper, not a universal author-identification guarantee.
papers.project_implication: Keep function-word summaries as descriptive comparisons, never identity proof.

verification.level: Opened proceedings metadata and primary PDF; inspected abstract and methodological discussion

papers.title: Deep Learning for Text Style Transfer: A Survey
papers.research_question: How is neural text style transfer formulated and evaluated?
papers.method: Surveys over 100 representative articles, datasets, methods, and evaluation approaches.
papers.key_findings: Style transfer spans multiple attributes and parallel/nonparallel data settings.
papers.limitations: Survey predates many instruction-tuned models; style labels simplify personal voice.
papers.project_implication: Specify desired changes and protected meaning separately.

papers.title: Evaluating Style Transfer for Text
papers.research_question: How should text style transfer be assessed?
papers.method: Yelp sentiment experiments compare human judgments and automatic measures.
papers.key_findings: Transfer intensity, content preservation, and naturalness trade off.
papers.limitations: Sentiment-transfer evidence does not directly validate individual-voice measures.
papers.project_implication: Report voice, fidelity, and readability separately; avoid one aggregate score.

papers.title: TextSETTR: Few-Shot Text Style Extraction and Tunable Targeted Restyling
papers.research_question: Can exemplars support targeted restyling without style-labeled training?
papers.method: T5-based style-vector extraction exploits adjacency in unlabeled text.
papers.key_findings: Few exemplars support changes across several tested stylistic dimensions.
papers.limitations: Benchmarks assess selected attributes, not complete personal identity or factual fidelity.
papers.project_implication: Use genre-matched exemplars and modest, explicit transfer goals.

papers.title: CoAuthor: Designing a Human-AI Collaborative Writing Dataset for Exploring Language Model Capabilities
papers.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’22)
papers.research_question: How can writing interactions expose language-model capabilities?
papers.method: Logs 1,445 creative/argumentative sessions from 63 writers with four GPT-3 instances.
papers.key_findings: Interaction traces support examining language, ideation, and collaboration contributions.
papers.limitations: Specific writers, tasks, interface, and historical model; no universal productivity estimate.
papers.project_implication: Preserve editable drafts and review decisions with explicit user consent.

papers.title: LaMP: When Large Language Models Meet Personalization
papers.research_question: Can profile retrieval improve personalized language tasks?
papers.method: Seven tasks evaluate personal-item retrieval with zero-shot and fine-tuned models.
papers.key_findings: Retrieval augmentation improves tested personalized classification and generation tasks.
papers.limitations: Task metrics do not establish authentic voice, privacy protection, or causality of every profile feature.
papers.project_implication: Retrieve relevant consented examples; test against no-profile and mismatched-profile baselines.

papers.title: DetectGPT: Zero-Shot Machine-Generated Text Detection using Probability Curvature
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 202, 24950–24962
papers.research_question: Can probability curvature separate generated and human passages?
papers.method: Compares source-model log probabilities against randomly perturbed passages.
papers.key_findings: GPT-NeoX fake-news AUROC increases from 0.81 baseline to 0.95.
papers.limitations: Requires model scoring and perturbation choices; benchmark discrimination is not authorship probability.
papers.project_implication: Do not use likelihood diagnostics as truth labels or revision objectives.

papers.title: Fast-DetectGPT: Efficient Zero-Shot Detection of Machine-Generated Text via Conditional Probability Curvature
papers.research_question: Can conditional scoring make curvature-based detection faster?
papers.method: Replaces passage perturbation with conditional token sampling/scoring.
papers.key_findings: Reports better AUROC and faster detection under tested model/domain conditions.
papers.limitations: Surrogate-model coverage varies across languages and domains; theoretical explanation remains incomplete.
papers.project_implication: Any research detector comparison needs matched models, thresholds, hardware, and language scope.

verification.level: Opened official conference PDF; inspected abstract, Table 1, and limitations
notes: The headline approximately 75% gain is (new AUROC − old AUROC)/(1 − old AUROC), not 75 percentage points of accuracy.
Reported 340× speedup uses XSum on a Tesla A100; it is not an application runtime promise.

papers.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
papers.publication_status: peer-reviewed journal opinion with empirical analyses
papers.research_question: Do tested detectors treat two English-writing cohorts differently?
papers.method: Seven detectors compare 91 TOEFL essays and 88 US school essays.
papers.key_findings: TOEFL essays have 61.3% average false positives in this comparison.
papers.limitations: Small, unmatched cohorts; no measured Indian-English subgroup or present-day detector guarantee.
papers.project_implication: Never infer authorship from predictability; audit language/register disparities.

verification.level: Opened archived published primary article; inspected cohort and results sections
notes: TOEFL essays were obtained from a Chinese forum; comparator essays were from US eighth-grade students.
Language-background attribution and genre/age/task differences limit causal interpretation.
The paper’s article type is Opinion, not a new general-population benchmark.

papers.title: Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text
papers.venue: International Journal for Educational Integrity, 19, article 26
papers.research_question: How reliably did the evaluated tools classify test documents?
papers.method: Tests 12 public tools and two commercial systems, including transformed text.
papers.key_findings: Tested systems show errors; obfuscation further worsens performance.
papers.limitations: Historical tool versions and document set do not rank current products.
papers.project_implication: Require current in-scope validation before any detector claim.

verification.level: Opened publisher full text and metadata

papers.title: Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected? Stress Testing AI Text Detectors Under Various Attacks
papers.research_question: How do editing attacks and distribution overlap constrain detection?
papers.method: Stress-tests detector families; derives a total-variation bound on AUROC.
papers.key_findings: Paraphrasing weakens tested signals; overlapping distributions limit discrimination.
papers.limitations: Theory is conditional on distributions; it does not prove every detector always fails.
papers.project_implication: Keep process provenance and fidelity checks independent of detector scores.

verification.level: Opened web-indexed accepted primary PDF and official TMLR publication listing
notes: Earlier 2023 arXiv versions had a shorter title. This record cites the 2025 accepted article.
Live canonical OpenReview URL displayed a browser challenge; the indexed accepted PDF text was accessible.
Official publication and complete author order verified at https://jmlr.org/tmlr/papers/.

papers.title: M4: Multi-generator, Multi-domain, and Multi-lingual Black-Box Machine-Generated Text Detection
papers.research_question: Do detectors generalize across generators, domains, and languages?
papers.method: Constructs and evaluates a multi-generator/domain/language detection corpus.
papers.key_findings: Unseen generators and domains cause substantial generalization difficulties.
papers.limitations: Benchmark coverage is finite and is not individual-language fairness validation.
papers.project_implication: Stratify evaluation; do not transfer English thresholds to all languages.

papers.title: Almost AI, Almost Human: The Challenge of Detecting AI-Polished Writing
papers.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025, 25414–25431
papers.research_question: Can detectors distinguish degrees of AI polishing?
papers.method: APT-Eval evaluates twelve detectors on 15K samples with varied AI involvement.
papers.key_findings: Minimal polishing can trigger flags; involvement levels are poorly separated.
papers.limitations: Controlled polishing procedures and evaluated versions do not cover every real workflow.
papers.project_implication: Describe actual editing operations instead of estimating an authorship percentage.

papers.title: Understanding the Effects of RLHF on LLM Generalisation and Diversity
papers.research_question: How do preference-training stages affect generalization and diversity?
papers.method: Compares SFT, RLHF, and best-of-N on two base models and two tasks.
papers.key_findings: RLHF improves tested generalization while reducing several diversity measures relative to SFT.
papers.limitations: Automatic metrics only; limited models/tasks; no universal mechanism or DPO result.
papers.project_implication: Measure voice variation across prompts and users, not average fluency alone.

verification.level: Opened official conference PDF; inspected abstract and Appendix A limitations

papers.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023)
papers.research_question: Can preference optimization avoid a separate reward-model training loop?
papers.method: Reparameterizes a KL-constrained reward objective as pairwise preference classification.
papers.key_findings: DPO simplifies preference training and performs well on tested alignment tasks.
papers.limitations: Does not establish that DPO causes generic prose or preserves personal voice.
papers.project_implication: Treat DPO as future optional training, requiring consented pairs and evaluation.

notes: Author order follows the opened current official NeurIPS proceedings record.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can preference judgments favor agreement over truth?
papers.method: Tests five assistants on four tasks; analyzes preferences and preference-model optimization.
papers.key_findings: Some convincing agreement is preferred despite incorrectness; optimization effects vary by behavior.
papers.limitations: Does not isolate DPO or prove all preference training produces sycophancy.
papers.project_implication: Separate tone matching from factual agreement; protect uncertainty and corrections.

verification.level: Opened official conference PDF; inspected abstract and introduction

papers.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
papers.research_question: Can excess vocabulary estimate corpus-level LLM-assisted writing?
papers.method: Compares 2010–2024 English PubMed abstract frequencies with extrapolated baselines.
papers.key_findings: Estimates a 13.5% lower bound for LLM-processed 2024 abstracts under its assumptions.
papers.limitations: Cannot identify individual abstracts or distinguish direct assistance from lexical diffusion.
papers.project_implication: Use vocabulary trends as context, never a banned-word or authorship rule.

verification.level: Opened archived published primary full text; inspected abstract and interpretation limitations
notes: Uses the 2025 published title and estimate, not the earlier 2024 preprint.
Country-level affiliation associations are not measurements of any individual’s linguistic ability.

papers.title: LinCE: A Centralized Benchmark for Linguistic Code-switching Evaluation
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Twelfth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference, 1803–1813
papers.research_question: How can code-switching NLP evaluation be standardized?
papers.method: Centralizes multiple corpora across four language pairs and four labeling tasks.
papers.key_findings: Includes Hindi–English and demonstrates a need for language/task-specific evaluation.
papers.limitations: Not a writing-assistance, Indian-English, or detector-fairness benchmark.
papers.project_implication: Preserve requested code-switching and evaluate it separately from monolingual prose.

notes: The landing abstract says eleven corpora while the PDF abstract says ten; no corpus-count claim is used here.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
papers.research_question: Why can high-likelihood decoding produce poor open-ended text?
papers.method: Compares decoding strategies using repetition, diversity, likelihood, and human evaluation.
papers.key_findings: Maximization can degenerate; nucleus sampling improves the tested quality/diversity tradeoff.
papers.limitations: Historical models and open-ended tasks; no universal best setting for factual rewriting.
papers.project_implication: Log decoding settings and compare outputs; randomness is not a fidelity guarantee.

verification.level: Opened institutional published primary PDF; inspected abstract and task distinction
notes: Canonical OpenReview page displayed a browser challenge; institutional PDF states publication at ICLR 2020.

papers.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
papers.research_question: Can strong models approximate human answer preferences?
papers.method: Introduces MT-Bench/Arena and compares model judgments with human preferences.
papers.key_findings: Strong agreement coexists with position, verbosity, self-enhancement, and reasoning biases.
papers.limitations: General answer preferences do not validate personal-voice or factual judgments.
papers.project_implication: Blind and randomize comparisons; retain author review and independent fidelity checks.
